terms.definition: A legal obligation to take reasonable care not to cause foreseeable harm to another person.
terms.examiner: Start with the neighbour principle in Donoghue v Stevenson. Since Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (2018) the courts look first to existing precedent or analogy, and use the Caparo approach only for novel situations.

terms.definition: Three stages for a novel duty situation: harm was reasonably foreseeable, there was proximity between the parties, and it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
terms.examiner: Caparo v Dickman, with a case for each stage: Kent v Griffiths (foreseeability), Bourhill v Young (proximity), Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (fair, just and reasonable).

terms.definition: Falling below the standard of care of the reasonable person.
terms.examiner: Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks. The test is objective: the defendant's own inexperience is no excuse (Nettleship v Weston).

terms.term: Standard of care: professionals, learners and children
terms.definition: A professional is judged by the standard of a competent member of that profession, a learner by the standard of the competent and experienced person, and a child by the standard of a reasonable child of the same age.
terms.examiner: Bolam (with Bolitho: the professional opinion must be logical), Nettleship v Weston, Mullin v Richards.

terms.definition: Matters that raise or lower the standard of care expected: the size of the risk, any special characteristics of the claimant, the cost and practicality of precautions, whether the risk was known, and any public benefit.
terms.examiner: A case for each: Bolton v Stone, Paris v Stepney, Latimer v AEC, Roe v Minister of Health, Watt v Hertfordshire County Council. Apply only the factors the scenario raises.

terms.definition: The "but for" test: the damage would not have happened but for the defendant's breach.
terms.examiner: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital: the patient would have died anyway, so the breach did not cause the death.

terms.definition: The damage must be of a type that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the breach.
terms.examiner: The Wagon Mound (No 1). The type must be foreseeable, not the exact way it happened or its extent (Hughes v Lord Advocate, Bradford v Robinson Rentals).

terms.definition: The defendant must take the claimant as they find them, and is liable for the full extent of the harm if the type of harm was foreseeable.
terms.examiner: Smith v Leech Brain: a burn triggered a cancer and the defendant was liable for the death.
